guides.bigIdea: Momentum is mass times velocity: a vector that points the way an object moves, and one that adds, direction included, to give the momentum of a whole system.

picture.diagram:
scene
ground 0..8
block A 2,0 "2 kg"
block B 6,0 "1 kg"
f A.t+0,0.35 right 1.5 "p_A = +6 kg·m/s"
f B.t+0,0.35 left 1 "p_B = -4 kg·m/s"
text 4,-0.7 "p_{sys} = +2 kg·m/s"
picture.caption: Taking right as positive, cart A has momentum $+6\ \text{kg·m/s}$ and cart B has $-4\ \text{kg·m/s}$. The system's momentum is their sum, $+2\ \text{kg·m/s}$, not 10.

guides.explanation:
Momentum answers a practical question: how much does it take to stop this thing? A bowling ball and a tennis ball rolling at the same speed are not equally easy to stop, and neither are two tennis balls at different speeds. Both mass and velocity matter, so momentum is defined as their product, $\vec{p} = m\vec{v}$, measured in $\text{kg·m/s}$. A $0.15\ \text{kg}$ baseball thrown at $40\ \text{m/s}$ and a $60\ \text{kg}$ skater drifting at $0.10\ \text{m/s}$ both carry $6.0\ \text{kg·m/s}$.

Because velocity is a vector, so is momentum, and it points the way the object is moving. In one dimension, choose a positive direction and let the sign carry the direction: a cart moving in the negative direction has negative momentum. That is not "less" momentum; it is momentum the other way.

The momentum of a system is the vector sum of the momenta of its parts, so signs matter. Two carts rolling toward each other partly cancel, and a system can have zero total momentum while everything in it is moving. The same care applies to a change in momentum, $\Delta\vec{p} = \vec{p}_f - \vec{p}_i$: a ball that reverses direction changes its momentum by more than a ball that merely stops, because it goes from positive, through zero, to negative.

equations.meaning: An object's momentum is its mass multiplied by its velocity, and it points the same way as the velocity.
equations.useWhen: You know, or want, the mass and velocity of one object at one instant.
equations.notWhen: Do not drop the direction when objects move different ways. And momentum is not a force: it is something a moving object has, not a push it gives.

equations.meaning: The momentum of a system is the sum of its objects' momenta, each with its own sign or direction.
equations.useWhen: You need the total momentum of two or more objects.
equations.notWhen: Do not add magnitudes. In two dimensions, add the x-components and the y-components separately.

equations.meaning: The change in an object's momentum is its final momentum minus its initial momentum.
equations.useWhen: One object's velocity changes: it speeds up, slows down, stops or bounces.
equations.notWhen: Do not subtract speeds when the direction reverses; the final velocity then has the opposite sign.

workedExamples.title: Momentum of a two-cart system
workedExamples.prompt: A $2.0\ \text{kg}$ cart moves to the right at $3.0\ \text{m/s}$. A $1.0\ \text{kg}$ cart moves to the left at $4.0\ \text{m/s}$. What is the momentum of the two-cart system?
steps: Choose a direction to call positive. Take right as positive, so the velocities are $v_A = +3.0\ \text{m/s}$ and $v_B = -4.0\ \text{m/s}$.
Find each cart's momentum: $p_A = (2.0\ \text{kg})(+3.0\ \text{m/s}) = +6.0\ \text{kg·m/s}$ and $p_B = (1.0\ \text{kg})(-4.0\ \text{m/s}) = -4.0\ \text{kg·m/s}$.
Add them, keeping the signs: $p_{\text{sys}} = +6.0 + (-4.0) = +2.0\ \text{kg·m/s}$.
Read the sign. Positive means the system's momentum points to the right, even though the faster cart is moving left.

workedExamples.title: A ball bouncing off a wall
workedExamples.prompt: A $0.060\ \text{kg}$ tennis ball travelling horizontally at $20\ \text{m/s}$ hits a wall and rebounds straight back at $15\ \text{m/s}$. Determine the change in the ball's momentum, and explain whether the change would be larger or smaller if the ball had stuck to the wall instead.
steps: Take the ball's original direction, toward the wall, as positive. Then $v_i = +20\ \text{m/s}$ and, because the ball comes back, $v_f = -15\ \text{m/s}$.
The negative sign says the change points away from the wall, which makes sense: the wall pushed the ball backward.

If the ball had stuck, its final momentum would be zero and the change would be $0 - (+1.2) = -1.2\ \text{kg·m/s}$. The bounce gives the larger change, because the ball's momentum is not just removed but reversed.
workedExamples.answer: $\Delta p = -2.1\ \text{kg·m/s}$, directed away from the wall; sticking would give only $-1.2\ \text{kg·m/s}$

misconceptions.wrong: Two carts heading toward each other with $6\ \text{kg·m/s}$ and $4\ \text{kg·m/s}$ have $10\ \text{kg·m/s}$ of momentum between them.
misconceptions.right: Momenta add as vectors. With right as positive the carts have $+6$ and $-4\ \text{kg·m/s}$, so the system has $+2\ \text{kg·m/s}$. Adding the sizes only works when everything moves the same way.

misconceptions.wrong: Momentum is just kinetic energy by another name, so doubling an object's speed quadruples its momentum.
misconceptions.right: Momentum is $mv$: double the speed and it doubles. Kinetic energy is $\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$: double the speed and it quadruples. Momentum also has a direction; kinetic energy does not.

misconceptions.wrong: The heavier object always has more momentum.
misconceptions.right: Momentum depends on mass and velocity together. A parked truck has zero momentum; a thrown baseball has more. Compare the products $mv$, not the masses.

checkYourself.q: A $1500\ \text{kg}$ car drives east at $20\ \text{m/s}$ and a $3000\ \text{kg}$ truck drives west at $10\ \text{m/s}$. What is the total momentum of the two vehicles?
checkYourself.a: Zero. With east as positive, the car has $+30\,000\ \text{kg·m/s}$ and the truck has $-30\,000\ \text{kg·m/s}$.

checkYourself.q: Can a single moving object have zero momentum? Can a system of moving objects?
checkYourself.a: One moving object cannot: its mass and its velocity are both non-zero. A system can, when its objects' momenta cancel, like the car and the truck above.

checkYourself.q: Ball X hits the floor and stops. An identical ball Y hits at the same speed and bounces back up. Which has the larger change in momentum?
checkYourself.a: Ball Y. X's momentum goes from $mv$ downward to zero, a change of size $mv$. Y's goes from $mv$ downward to some momentum upward, a change larger than $mv$ (up to $2mv$).

tryIt.caption: Change the cart's mass and velocity. The momentum arrow grows with either one, and flips when the velocity changes sign.

guides.teacherNotes: Students arrive with "momentum" as an everyday word for being hard to stop, and usually treat it as a positive amount. Insist on a stated positive direction and signed velocities from the first example: most later errors in this unit (bounces, head-on collisions) trace back to dropped signs. A quick whiteboard check is two carts with momenta $+6$ and $-4$; anyone who answers 10 needs the vector idea again before impulse.

guides.bigIdea: A net force acting over a time interval delivers an impulse, and that impulse equals the change in the object's momentum.

picture.diagram:
plot x=t[s] y=F[N] xr=0,0.03 yr=0,700
seg 0,0 0.01,600 0.02,0
shade 0..0.02
note 0.021,400 "area = impulse"
picture.caption: A bat's force on a ball rises and falls in about $0.02\ \text{s}$. The shaded area under the force–time graph is the impulse: $\tfrac{1}{2}(0.02\ \text{s})(600\ \text{N}) = 6\ \text{N·s}$.

guides.explanation:
Newton's second law says a net force changes an object's velocity. Write the acceleration as $\Delta\vec{v}/\Delta t$ and rearrange: $\vec{F}_{\text{net}}\,\Delta t = m\,\Delta\vec{v} = \Delta\vec{p}$. The left side, force multiplied by the time it acts, is the impulse, $\vec{J}$, and the result is the impulse–momentum theorem: impulse equals change in momentum. The units agree: $1\ \text{N·s} = 1\ \text{kg·m/s}$.

The theorem explains every "soften the blow" design. A rider who goes from $5\ \text{m/s}$ to rest has the same change in momentum whether they hit a wall or a crash mat, so the impulse is the same. What changes is the time: the mat stretches the stop out, and because $F_{\text{avg}} = \Delta p/\Delta t$, a longer time means a smaller average force. Airbags and bent knees on landing work the same way.

Real collision forces are not constant; they rise to a peak and fall away. Impulse is then the area under the force–time graph, and the average force is the steady force that would give the same area in the same time. Read the other way, the net force on an object is the rate at which its momentum changes: the slope of its momentum–time graph.

equations.meaning: Impulse is the average force multiplied by the time it acts, and it points the way the force does.
equations.useWhen: The force is steady, or you are given or asked for the average force over a known time.
equations.notWhen: If the force changes and you have a force–time graph, use the area under the graph instead.

equations.meaning: The impulse from the net force on an object equals the change in its momentum.
equations.useWhen: You know the velocities before and after and want the impulse or average force, or you know the impulse and want a final velocity.
equations.notWhen: Do not use the impulse of one force when others also act; the theorem needs the net force. And keep the signs: a rebound makes $v_f$ and $v_i$ opposite.

equations.meaning: The net force on an object is the rate of change of its momentum (the average net force, if the force varies).
equations.useWhen: Comparing stops or hits with the same change in momentum over different times, or reading force from the slope of a momentum–time graph.
equations.notWhen: It gives the average over the interval, not the peak force of a collision, which is larger.

workedExamples.title: Average force on a batted ball
workedExamples.prompt: A $0.145\ \text{kg}$ baseball reaches the bat at $38\ \text{m/s}$ and leaves in the opposite direction at $52\ \text{m/s}$. The ball and bat are in contact for $0.0015\ \text{s}$. What average force does the bat exert on the ball?
steps: Take the direction the ball leaves as positive. Then $v_i = -38\ \text{m/s}$ and $v_f = +52\ \text{m/s}$.
Find the change in momentum: $\Delta p = m(v_f - v_i) = (0.145\ \text{kg})\big(52 - (-38)\big)\ \text{m/s} = (0.145)(90) = 13.05\ \text{kg·m/s}$. Keep the extra digits until the end.
The impulse on the ball equals this change, so $F_{\text{avg}}\,\Delta t = 13.05\ \text{N·s}$.
Divide by the contact time: $F_{\text{avg}} = \dfrac{13.05\ \text{N·s}}{0.0015\ \text{s}} = 8.7 \times 10^3\ \text{N}$.
Check: that is thousands of times the ball's weight (about $1.4\ \text{N}$), which is why the weight can be ignored during the hit.
workedExamples.answer: $F_{\text{avg}} = 8.7 \times 10^3\ \text{N}$, in the direction the ball leaves

workedExamples.title: Impulse from a force–time graph
workedExamples.prompt:
A $0.50\ \text{kg}$ cart is at rest on a level, low-friction track. A student pushes it with a horizontal force that varies as shown: it rises steadily to $6.0\ \text{N}$ over the first $0.10\ \text{s}$, stays at $6.0\ \text{N}$ for $0.20\ \text{s}$, then falls steadily to zero over the last $0.10\ \text{s}$. Determine the cart's speed when the push ends.

```dg
plot x=t[s] y=F[N] xr=0,0.45 yr=0,7
seg 0,0 0.1,6 0.3,6 0.4,0
xt 0 0.1 0.2 0.3 0.4
yt 0 2 4 6
```
steps: The force is not constant, so the impulse is the area under the force–time graph. Split the area into a triangle, a rectangle and a second triangle.
The track is level and low-friction, so the push is the net force and its impulse equals the cart's change in momentum: $J = m v_f - m v_i$, with $v_i = 0$.
$v_f = \dfrac{J}{m} = \dfrac{1.8\ \text{N·s}}{0.50\ \text{kg}} = 3.6\ \text{m/s}$, in the direction of the push.

misconceptions.wrong: An airbag protects you by reducing the impulse in a crash.
misconceptions.right: Your change in momentum is fixed: you start at the car's speed and end at rest, so the impulse is the same with or without the airbag. The airbag lengthens the stop, which makes the average force smaller.

misconceptions.wrong: The larger force always delivers the larger impulse.
misconceptions.right: Impulse is force multiplied by time. A $2\ \text{N}$ push held for $10\ \text{s}$ delivers $20\ \text{N·s}$, four times the impulse of a $50\ \text{N}$ tap that lasts $0.1\ \text{s}$.

misconceptions.wrong: A ball that bounces back at the speed it arrived with has no change in momentum, so the wall gave it no impulse.
misconceptions.right: Its speed is unchanged but its velocity reversed, so $\Delta p = m(-v) - m(v) = -2mv$. The wall delivers twice the impulse it would need just to stop the ball.

checkYourself.q: Why does landing with bent knees hurt less than landing stiff-legged from the same height?
checkYourself.a: Either way you arrive with the same momentum and end at rest, so the impulse is the same. Bent knees spread the stop over a longer time, so the average force on your legs is smaller.

checkYourself.q: A net force of $4\ \text{N}$ acts for $3\ \text{s}$ on a $2\ \text{kg}$ cart that starts at rest. What impulse does it deliver, and how fast is the cart moving afterwards?
checkYourself.a: $J = (4\ \text{N})(3\ \text{s}) = 12\ \text{N·s}$. That equals the change in momentum, so $v = (12\ \text{kg·m/s})/(2\ \text{kg}) = 6\ \text{m/s}$.

checkYourself.q: A cart's momentum rises steadily from $2\ \text{kg·m/s}$ to $8\ \text{kg·m/s}$ in $3\ \text{s}$. What net force acts on it?
checkYourself.a: $2\ \text{N}$. The net force is the slope of the momentum–time graph: $(8 - 2)\ \text{kg·m/s}$ divided by $3\ \text{s}$.

tryIt.caption: Stopping a $60\ \text{kg}$ rider moving at $5\ \text{m/s}$ always takes $300\ \text{N·s}$. Change the stopping time and watch the average force; the area stays the same.

guides.teacherNotes: The persistent error is "the airbag reduces the impulse". Have students compute $\Delta p$ for a hard stop and a soft stop and see that it is the same number before anyone talks about force. With force–time graphs, ask for the area in words ("newtons times seconds") so it is not confused with the slope. Set 4B practises both.

guides.bigIdea: If no net external force acts on a system, its total momentum does not change, no matter what the objects inside it do to one another.

picture.diagram:
scene
text 1,3.3 "Before: at rest"
ground 0..8 y=2
block A 3.5,2 "1 kg"
block B 4.5,2 "2 kg"
text 0.5,1.3 "After"
ground 0..8
block C 2,0 "1 kg"
block D 5.8,0 "2 kg"
f C.t+0,0.3 left 1.6 "4 m/s"
f D.t+0,0.3 right 0.8 "2 m/s"
picture.caption: Two carts at rest are pushed apart by a spring. The total momentum is zero before and after: the $1\ \text{kg}$ cart leaves at $4\ \text{m/s}$ one way and the $2\ \text{kg}$ cart at $2\ \text{m/s}$ the other, so $-4 + 4 = 0\ \text{kg·m/s}$.

guides.explanation:
When two objects in a system push on each other, Newton's third law says the forces are equal in size, opposite in direction and last exactly the same time. So the impulses are equal and opposite: whatever momentum one object gains, the other loses. Forces inside a system move momentum from one part to another but cannot change the total.

Only a net external force, from something outside the system, can do that. If there is none, or its impulse is negligible during a brief collision, the system is isolated and its total momentum stays constant. So the choice of system matters. For two carts on a level, low-friction track, gravity and the normal force cancel and the forces between the carts are internal: the pair's momentum is conserved. For one cart alone, the other cart's push is external, and that cart's momentum changes.

To use the idea, pick a positive direction, write the total momentum before, set it equal to the total after, and solve. It works for collisions and for "explosions", where objects at rest push apart: the total stays zero, so they leave with equal and opposite momenta and the lighter one moves faster.

The system's centre of mass moves with velocity $\vec{v}_{\text{cm}} = \vec{p}_{\text{sys}}/M$, where $M$ is the total mass, so it keeps a constant velocity straight through a collision.

equations.meaning: For an isolated system of two objects, the total momentum before an interaction equals the total after.
equations.useWhen: Collisions, pushes apart and explosions where the net external force is zero or negligible during the interaction.
equations.notWhen: Not for one object on its own, and not when an outside force such as friction acts for a significant time.

equations.meaning: The centre of mass moves at the system's total momentum divided by its total mass.

variables.name: velocity of the centre of mass
velocities of the objects at the same instant

equations.useWhen: You want the velocity of the system as a whole, or a quick check: it is the same before and after an isolated interaction.
equations.notWhen: It is not any one object's velocity, unless the objects move together.

equations.meaning: If a net external force does act, the system's momentum changes by that force's impulse.

variables.name: change in the system's total momentum
average net external force on the system

equations.useWhen: The system is not isolated: friction, an outside push or gravity acts during the interval.
equations.notWhen: Do not count forces between objects inside the system; they cancel in pairs.

workedExamples.title: Two skaters push apart
workedExamples.prompt: Two ice skaters stand at rest, facing each other. Skater A has mass $50\ \text{kg}$ and skater B has mass $75\ \text{kg}$. They push off each other, and A glides to the left at $1.8\ \text{m/s}$. What is B's velocity? Ignore friction with the ice.
steps: Choose the system: both skaters. Their pushes on each other are internal, and with no friction there is no net external force, so momentum is conserved.
Take right as positive. Before the push both skaters are at rest, so the total momentum is zero. After it, $v_A = -1.8\ \text{m/s}$.
Write momentum before = momentum after: $0 = m_A v_A + m_B v_B = (50\ \text{kg})(-1.8\ \text{m/s}) + (75\ \text{kg})\,v_B$.
Solve: $(75\ \text{kg})\,v_B = +90\ \text{kg·m/s}$, so $v_B = +1.2\ \text{m/s}$.
Check: the momenta are $-90$ and $+90\ \text{kg·m/s}$, equal and opposite, and the heavier skater is the slower one.

workedExamples.title: A collision where the carts bounce apart
workedExamples.prompt: Cart 1 ($0.50\ \text{kg}$) moves to the right at $2.0\ \text{m/s}$ on a level, low-friction track and hits cart 2 ($1.5\ \text{kg}$), which is at rest. Afterwards cart 1 moves to the left at $0.40\ \text{m/s}$. Determine cart 2's velocity after the collision, and show that the centre of mass has the same velocity before and after.
steps: System: the two carts. The track is level and low-friction, so the net external force is zero and momentum is conserved. Take right as positive.
Before: $p_i = (0.50\ \text{kg})(+2.0\ \text{m/s}) + 0 = +1.0\ \text{kg·m/s}$.
Setting $p_f = p_i$ gives $(1.5\ \text{kg})\,v_{2f} = 1.0 + 0.20 = 1.2\ \text{kg·m/s}$, so $v_{2f} = +0.80\ \text{m/s}$.

Centre of mass: before, $v_{\text{cm}} = (1.0\ \text{kg·m/s})/(2.0\ \text{kg}) = 0.50\ \text{m/s}$. After, $v_{\text{cm}} = (-0.20 + 1.2)/2.0 = 0.50\ \text{m/s}$, unchanged, as it must be for an isolated system.

misconceptions.wrong: Cart 1 slowed down in the collision, so some momentum was lost.
misconceptions.right: Cart 1's momentum did go down, because cart 2 pushed on it; for cart 1 alone that push is an external force. The momentum was not lost but transferred to cart 2. The total for the two-cart system stays the same.

misconceptions.wrong: In a collision the heavier or faster object pushes harder, so it gives more momentum than it gets.
misconceptions.right: The two forces are a third-law pair: equal in size at every instant, for the same time. So the impulses are equal and opposite, and the momentum one object gains is exactly what the other loses. The lighter object's velocity changes more, not its momentum.

misconceptions.wrong: Momentum is always conserved, so a dropped ball's momentum stays the same as it falls.
misconceptions.right: Conservation needs a system with no net external force. For the ball alone, gravity is external and its momentum grows. Include the Earth in the system and the total is conserved again: the Earth gains an equal and opposite (unnoticeable) momentum.

checkYourself.q: An astronaut floating at rest beside a space station throws a wrench directly away from the station. What happens to the astronaut, and why?
checkYourself.a: The astronaut drifts toward the station. Astronaut and wrench start with zero total momentum and no external force acts, so the total stays zero: the astronaut gets momentum equal and opposite to the wrench's, at a much smaller speed.

checkYourself.q: A $1\ \text{kg}$ cart moving at $4\ \text{m/s}$ hits a $3\ \text{kg}$ cart at rest and sticks to it. How fast do they move together?
checkYourself.a: The momentum before is $4\ \text{kg·m/s}$ and the combined mass is $4\ \text{kg}$, so they move at $1\ \text{m/s}$ in the first cart's original direction.

checkYourself.q: Two carts collide on a track with noticeable friction. Is the two-cart system's momentum conserved during the collision? Over the next few seconds?
checkYourself.a: During the brief collision, very nearly: friction's impulse is tiny in so short a time. Over several seconds, no: friction is an external force and steadily removes momentum from the system.

tryIt.caption: Two skaters push apart from rest. Skater A ($60\ \text{kg}$) always leaves at $2\ \text{m/s}$. Change skater B's mass: B's speed changes, but the two momenta stay equal and opposite.

guides.teacherNotes: Make students name the system and say why it is isolated before they write an equation; free-response scoring usually rewards exactly that sentence. A useful contrast is to analyse the same collision twice, once with both carts as the system (momentum conserved) and once with a single cart (its momentum changes by the other cart's impulse). Set 4C includes pushes apart and centre-of-mass questions.

guides.bigIdea: Momentum is conserved in every collision between objects in an isolated system, but kinetic energy is conserved only when the collision is elastic.

picture.caption: A $2\ \text{kg}$ cart moving at $3\ \text{m/s}$ runs into a $1\ \text{kg}$ cart at rest and they lock together, sharing $2\ \text{m/s}$ afterwards. The momentum is $6\ \text{kg·m/s}$ before and after, but the kinetic energy falls from $9\ \text{J}$ to $6\ \text{J}$.

guides.explanation:
During a collision the forces between the objects are large and brief, so outside forces have almost no time to deliver an impulse. That is why momentum is conserved in collisions of every kind. What sorts collisions into types is what happens to the system's kinetic energy.

In an elastic collision the total kinetic energy is the same after as before; billiard balls and carts with magnetic bumpers come close. In an inelastic collision some kinetic energy is transformed into thermal energy, sound and permanent deformation. Total energy is still conserved, just no longer all as kinetic energy. If the objects stick together, the collision is perfectly inelastic, and it loses as much kinetic energy as conservation of momentum allows.

That limit matters. Objects that stick together still carry the system's momentum, so they keep moving and some kinetic energy remains. All of it can go only when the total momentum is zero, as when two equal lumps of clay meet head-on at equal speeds.

You cannot tell the type by looking. Use conservation of momentum to find the unknown velocity, then compare the total kinetic energy before and after. One handy elastic result: two objects of equal mass simply exchange velocities.

equations.meaning: In a perfectly inelastic collision the objects leave together, so one final velocity carries all of the momentum.
equations.useWhen: The objects stick together, couple or embed: a caught ball, coupled rail cars, lumps of clay.
equations.notWhen: Not when the objects separate afterwards; then each needs its own final velocity.

equations.meaning: In an elastic collision the total kinetic energy before equals the total after.
equations.useWhen: Only when the collision is stated or shown to be elastic, and together with conservation of momentum.
equations.notWhen: Never assume it. If the objects stick or deform, or the problem does not say elastic, kinetic energy is not conserved.

equations.meaning: The change in the system's total kinetic energy gives the type of collision: zero for elastic, negative for inelastic.
equations.useWhen: Classifying a collision, or finding how much kinetic energy was transformed into other forms.
equations.notWhen: It says nothing about momentum, which is conserved either way. Each $K$ is $\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$ added over the objects, never $mv$.

workedExamples.title: Kinetic energy lost when carts stick
workedExamples.prompt: A $2.0\ \text{kg}$ cart moving at $3.0\ \text{m/s}$ collides with a $1.0\ \text{kg}$ cart at rest on a level, low-friction track. The carts lock together. How much kinetic energy is transformed into other forms in the collision?
steps: The carts stick, so the collision is perfectly inelastic: momentum is conserved, kinetic energy is not.
Momentum before: $(2.0\ \text{kg})(3.0\ \text{m/s}) + 0 = 6.0\ \text{kg·m/s}$.
After, the carts move as one object of mass $3.0\ \text{kg}$: $(3.0\ \text{kg})\,v_f = 6.0\ \text{kg·m/s}$, so $v_f = 2.0\ \text{m/s}$.
Kinetic energy before: $K_i = \tfrac{1}{2}(2.0\ \text{kg})(3.0\ \text{m/s})^2 = 9.0\ \text{J}$. After: $K_f = \tfrac{1}{2}(3.0\ \text{kg})(2.0\ \text{m/s})^2 = 6.0\ \text{J}$.
Subtract: $K_i - K_f = 9.0 - 6.0 = 3.0\ \text{J}$. One third of the kinetic energy has become thermal energy, sound and deformation, while all of the momentum is still there.
workedExamples.answer: $3.0\ \text{J}$ of kinetic energy is transformed (from $9.0\ \text{J}$ to $6.0\ \text{J}$)

workedExamples.title: Is this collision elastic?
workedExamples.prompt: Puck A, of mass $0.20\ \text{kg}$, slides at $5.0\ \text{m/s}$ on an air table and hits puck B, of mass $0.30\ \text{kg}$, which is at rest. Afterwards A moves backward at $1.0\ \text{m/s}$ and B moves forward at $4.0\ \text{m/s}$. Is the collision elastic? Justify your answer with a calculation.
steps: A collision is elastic if the total kinetic energy is the same before and after, so compare the two totals. Momentum cannot decide it; it is conserved either way (here $+1.0\ \text{kg·m/s}$ before and $-0.20 + 1.2 = +1.0\ \text{kg·m/s}$ after).
Before: $K_i = \tfrac{1}{2}(0.20\ \text{kg})(5.0\ \text{m/s})^2 = 2.5\ \text{J}$.
The totals are equal, so the collision is elastic. Direction does not enter: kinetic energy depends on speed squared, so A's backward motion still counts as positive.
workedExamples.answer: Yes, it is elastic: the total kinetic energy is $2.5\ \text{J}$ both before and after

misconceptions.wrong: Momentum is conserved in this collision, so kinetic energy must be conserved too.
misconceptions.right: They are different quantities with different rules. Momentum is conserved in any collision of an isolated system; kinetic energy only in elastic ones. Calculate it before and after to find out.

misconceptions.wrong: Energy is lost in an inelastic collision, so momentum is lost as well.
misconceptions.right: Kinetic energy can turn into thermal energy and sound, but momentum has no other form to turn into. With no external impulse, the total momentum is exactly what it was.

misconceptions.wrong: The kinetic energy missing after an inelastic collision has simply disappeared.
misconceptions.right: Energy is conserved. The missing kinetic energy went into warming and deforming the objects and into sound.

misconceptions.wrong: Perfectly inelastic means the objects stop dead.
misconceptions.right: It means they stick together and share one velocity. They stop only if the total momentum was zero.

checkYourself.q: A cart rolls into an identical cart at rest, and the collision is elastic. Describe the motion afterwards.
checkYourself.a: The moving cart stops and the other moves off with the first cart's original velocity. Equal masses exchange velocities, which conserves both momentum and kinetic energy.

checkYourself.q: Two equal lumps of clay fly toward each other at the same speed and stick. What is their velocity afterwards, and where did the kinetic energy go?
checkYourself.a: Zero: the total momentum was zero before, so it is zero after. All of the kinetic energy became thermal energy, deformation and sound.

checkYourself.q: Two carts are held together with a compressed spring between them, then released. The total kinetic energy afterwards is greater than before. Does this break a conservation law?
checkYourself.a: No. Momentum is conserved: zero before and after. The extra kinetic energy came from elastic potential energy stored in the spring, so total energy is conserved too.

tryIt.caption: A $2\ \text{kg}$ cart at $3\ \text{m/s}$ sticks to a target cart at rest. Make the target heavier: the final speed drops and less kinetic energy survives, yet the total momentum is $6\ \text{kg·m/s}$ every time.

guides.teacherNotes: Students tend to hold one of two mirror-image errors: "momentum is conserved, so energy is" or "energy is lost, so momentum is". Asking for both totals, before and after, on every collision problem for a week is the most reliable cure. In this algebra-based course students are not expected to solve the two elastic equations simultaneously in general; they should be able to check whether a given outcome is elastic and to use the equal-mass result. Set 4D mixes sticking and bouncing collisions.
